Issued at 158 AM MDT Fri Oct 9 2026

For those of us that like warm weather, this has been a very 
enjoyable past couple of weeks. The area has received very little 
rain over the past couple of weeks, and temperatures have been nice 
and warm, but not hot. And still comfortably cool at night as well. 
However, all good things must come to an end, and it looks like this 
will occur over the weekend as we transition into a cooler and 
wetter pattern. We do need the rain though.

We will have one more very warm day today. Most locations below 5500 
feet should see high temperatures into the 80s today. The difference 
today is that there will be breezy to windy conditions developing 
across much of the area ahead of a strong cold front approaching the 
area from the north. With the pressure gradient tightening ahead of 
the front, almost the entire area has at least a 1 out of 2 chance 
of wind gusts over 30 mph. The limiting factor will be humidity. The 
mean low humidity on the NBM ensemble less than 15 percent covers 
the northeastern half of the area as well as eastern Sweetwater 
County. With this, we have expanded the Red Flag Warning to cover 
the Bighorn Basin, Cody Foothills, the Owl Creek and Bridger 
Mountains as well as the southern Bighorn Range. However, all 
areas will have at least elevated fire weather this afternoon. 

The transition day will be Saturday. We have the same three 
players that will impact the weather: the cold front approaching
from the north, an upper level low over the Pacific Northwest 
and the remnants of Hurricane Rachel that will be drawn 
northward into the area. Shower and thunderstorm development 
will increase on Saturday, especially in the afternoon and 
evening as deeper moisture gets drawn into the area. Some 
guidance shows precipitable water rising as high as 0.80 inches 
by Sunday morning. This is more than 200 percent of the 
climatological mean and would be a record for the date. The core
of any forcing should remain south of the area though, so 
shower coverage would be more scattered, with the greatest 
coverage in the western mountains. There will be one more warm 
day east of the Divide, although somewhat cooler with increased 
cloud cover across the area. Shower coverage may increase at 
night when deeper moisture moves toward the area and whatever is
left of the circulation from Rachel approaches the area.

Sunday still looks like the wettest day across the area, as the
deepest moisture from Rachel makes its closest approach. There 
has been some change though. The most recent guidance takes the 
deepest moisture and best forcing further to the west, which may
lower precipitation amounts across portions of the area, 
especially east of the Divide. And, with cooler temperatures 
and more extensive cloud cover, the precipitation may be more 
stratiform and not convective. The Weather Prediction Center did
cut back the marginal risk of Excessive Rainfall somewhat as a 
result, confining it largely to far western Wyoming. There is 
fair agreement in showing the wettest period from Sunday 
afternoon through Sunday evening, when the circulation makes 
its closest approach and we get additional jet dynamics from 
the right rear quadrant of a jet streak moving across the 
Montana / Wyoming border. As for snow, there will be some. I 
will discuss this later in the discussion.

Following this, uncertainty ramps up across the forecast. The X
factor is how fast will the upper level low now located over 
the Pacific Northwest move through the area. As for the 
deterministic models, the ECMWF is around 18 to 24 hours faster
than the GFS. For example, the ECMWF keeps showers going 
through Monday night into Tuesday, while the GFS is largely dry.
The GFS also lingers showers longer into Wednesday night, while
the ECMWF dries things out faster. It does look unsettled 
through Wednesday, but details in precipitation amounts, 
placement of the heaviest precipitation and timing remain highly
uncertain for this time frame at this time.

As for total rainfall amounts, most areas should have a decent 
chance of rain. I will only discuss amounts through 6 am Monday, as 
uncertainty really increases past that. All areas across western and 
central Wyoming have at least a 1 in 2 chance of having at least a 
quarter of an inch or QPF through Monday morning, with the highest 
chance in western Wyoming. As for an inch of QPF, the area north and 
west of a Cokeville to Dubois to Clark line has at least a 1 in 2 
chance of this, with rapidly decreasing chances further east. The 
real epicenters of the heaviest QPF at this time look to be the 
favored southwest flow areas like the Wind River Range, Tetons and 
Yellowstone Park. Some of the highest elevations here have a 1 in 2 
chance of 2 inches or more of QPF. As for the risk of flooding, it 
is there. There are some mitigating factors. For one, it has been
